The Affirmative Action Problem

Graph TheoryLogicInvariants
Game: Colour the dots so that each one touches at least as many opposite-colour dots as same-colour dots.
How to play: Click a dot to switch black and white. Drag between dots to join them, or press "Find colouring" to let the rule do the work.
Look for the math

Can every graph be coloured black and white so that no dot is outnumbered by its own kind? The surprising answer is yes, and the proof fits in one line: make as many edges join different colours as possible.

Integrated dots

A dot is integrated when at least half of its neighbours have the other colour — a white dot needs at least as many black neighbours as white ones, and a black dot needs at least as many white ones as black. Colour the whole graph this way and every dot is content. Loops are not allowed: a dot is not its own neighbour.

Maximise balanced edges

Call an edge balanced when its two ends have different colours. There are finitely many colourings, so one of them has the most balanced edges. Suppose a dot in such a colouring were not integrated. More of its edges would join same colours than different ones. Flipping just that dot would turn all those same-colour edges balanced and the previously balanced ones same — so the total would go up, contradicting maximality. Hence every dot is integrated. This proof is due to Jim Propp.

What the check found

The logic test examines every simple graph with at most five nodes and every one of its colourings — 1,099 graphs in all. Every graph has an integrated colouring, every colouring with the most balanced edges is integrated, and flipping any non-integrated dot gains exactly the predicted number of balanced edges. The board here starts as a twenty-node grid with horizontal and vertical edges, close to the applet's opening picture; the applet also draws three families of diagonals.

Press "Find colouring" and watch the highlighted balanced edges. Can you then flip one dot without lowering their count?
